newsitem.title: INDIA: Top Indian bourses battle it out to reach investors.
newsitem.headline: Top Indian bourses battle it out to reach investors.

text.p: India's two biggest bourses plan to rapidly expand through a national network of on-line trade as each races the other to boost business and grab investors, officials said on Thursday.
"We plan to begin our first trading centre outside Bombay by the end of February," Madan Gopal Damani, president of the 122-year-old Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE), told Reuters.
The Securities & Exchange Board of India, the market regulator, removed the last obstacle to the BSE's setting up terminals across the nation when it approved expansion plans last October.
"We are going all out to take on the competition," Damani said. The BSE plans to operate from 135 centres by March 1997.
But it faces stiff competition from the rival National Stock Exchange (NSE), the pioneer of Indian electronic trading launched in September 1994, which plans to capitalise on its early start.
"We are pushing ahead very strongly so that benefits of added transparency are made available to as many investor pockets as possible," said NSE deputy managing director Ravi Narain.
The exchange, also based in Bombay, now runs 82 centres across India, of which 37 were added in 1997 alone, Narain said. "We plan to operate from 100 centres by the end of March," he added.
Each of the two exchanges hopes to edge out the other in its rush to scoop up the 20 million investors who trade on India's 23 stock exchanges.

BSE's Damani said a 1.7-billion-rupee ($47.4 million) trade guarantee fund was scheduled to shortly begin safeguarding all transactions between members as a pre-condition to expanding the bourse's nationwide network.
The BSE lists 6,800 stocks, with a daily turnover of seven to 10 billion rupees. About 1,500 securities are traded at the NSE, which has a daily turnover of 12-15 billion rupees.
BSE officials said the expansion would improve liquidity in about a quarter of the stocks which currently go untraded due to mismatched orders.
Welcoming the BSE's plan to establish trading terminals outside Bombay, NSE's Narain said it would usher in healthy competition among Indian exchanges.
"It's very good. This finally offers investors a choice to judge the two systems," Narain said.

BSE's Damani said a final agreement with the Calcutta Stock Exchange would be signed by mid-February. Regional bourses like Ahmedabad in the western state of Gujarat and the smaller Pune exchange had approached him to work with the BSE, he said.
"Any monopoly is unwise. Ultimately, when a second product is available, it will not take time before investors switch from a particular exchange," Damani said.
"We are targeting the three T's -- trust, transparency and tradition -- that the BSE enjoys."
